items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Mr. Wallerstein ... was the man who hired me to do that great series of the Hot Jazz Classics reissues.

ctx.x: Did you personally have — I don’t want to say a problem — how did you adjust in your thinking and listening to the bop movement?

Oh that was a kind of an interesting thing because I was already aware of what was beginning to happen before the war. You see I got drafted straight off the campus, I was inducted about two or three months after I graduated from Yale. The first inkling was in the form of Dizzy Gillespie’s playing. And I first heard Dizzy in I guess it was 1938 because I remember discussing it with Marshall Stearns. His records came out and there were solos of Dizzy’s on various releases, including of course the Cab Calloway…

discharged relatively early, in fact he got discharged when his squadron was brought back to the United States from Europe in order to fly out immediately to Japan and then they were told when they were ready to go, well we don’t need you out there and those of you who have had enough service can get discharged. And that’s when he married my sister and moved out to Los Angeles, his home. items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Mr. Wallerstein asked me to come to Columbia once a week. I would get paid $25 for researching – a week – for researching the material that they had and getting test pressings and deciding what to put out.

ctx.x: Bill Russell – I hope that somebody writes a book about him. I don’t know who’s going to do it. Bill Russell was a classically trained violinist who became, or tried to become, a contemporary classical composer. I don’t know how much he wrote, but he went into a branch, which we’ll get into in a second, which was extraordinary. His name was Russell Wagner. He changed his name to William Russell because he didn’t want to sign his scores “R. Wagner.” Bill turned to something which he was inspired to do by…

Juilliard to perform a Russian concerto at a program at the Juilliard School put on for Russian war relief, she had the very interesting idea of not performing the Tchaikovsky or Rachmaninoff or Prokofiev concertos, one of them, but instead find a new composer who was more representative of the spirit of that program, which was to solidify the Soviet and American fight against Fascism and Hitler. She came across the name Khachaturian, looked up the concerto, and saw, wow, it’s really fine. He’s Armenian. Great.…
